title: Fleet platform: what shape it should have
subtitle: The architecture style for the next Acme Logistics system, decided from the brief by eliminating options.

verdict.text: Build the fleet platform as services with an event backbone: four deployables around five business areas, with telemetry ingestion and route optimisation each running alone. The binding constraint is who can run it, because 2 platform engineers is one short of the 3 that microservices need.

items: Business areas
5. Only two parts are named: vehicle telemetry ingestion and route optimisation. Source: `fleet-platform.md:8`, `:9`, `:11` [high]
Teams
4 product teams with 30 engineers. Source: `fleet-platform.md:7` [high]
Who runs production
2 platform engineers. The brief does not say who is on call. Source: `fleet-platform.md:7` [high]
How often parts change
The teams ship on their own schedules. No release frequency is given. Source: `fleet-platform.md:10` [high]
Load per part
Telemetry ingestion takes about 200 times the load of the rest, steady day and night. No absolute rates are given. Source: `fleet-platform.md:9`, `:14` [high]
Runtimes
Route optimisation is in Python, the rest is .NET. Source: `fleet-platform.md:11` [high]
Long work
Route computations run for up to 40 minutes. Source: `fleet-platform.md:15` [high]
Shared events
Several teams must react to the same vehicle events. Source: `fleet-platform.md:12` [high]
Consistency
No transaction spans two business areas. Source: `fleet-platform.md:13` [high]
Not negotiable
The brief names no compliance, region, budget or deadline limit, so nothing beyond the facts above is treated as fixed. Source: not stated in `fleet-platform.md` [high]

sections.title: Assumptions
sections.intro: All ten facts the hard rules read come straight from the brief, so no rule rests on an assumption. The assumptions below shape the boundaries and how the chosen option is run.

items: **The five areas are telemetry, route optimisation and three the brief does not name**, shown here as Area C, D and E. Drives: the boundaries. No decision depends on what C, D and E turn out to be, as long as they are .NET at ordinary load. [guess]
**Telemetry and route optimisation have one team each, and the other two teams share C, D and E, with C and D on one team.** Drives: four deployables rather than five. [guess]
**Only derived vehicle events go on the backbone, and raw telemetry stays inside ingestion.** Drives: the 200 times load stays in one part and the backbone is sized for events. [guess]
**The broker is a managed service, with no vendor chosen yet.** Drives: rating "can this team run it" as weak rather than fail. [guess]
**Each product team is on call for its own services, and the platform engineers run the broker, the deployment path and tracing.** Drives: the same rating. [guess]

**A route computation is a job: the request is accepted at once, the result is published as an event, and a job can resume from a checkpoint.** Drives: the route optimisation boundary and how it deploys. [med]

sections.title: Decision
sections.intro: Options run from the simplest up. The hard rules come first, then the factors in order: the first factor that rules an option out eliminates it.

options.label: One deployable
options.why: Parts must release on their own schedules, one part takes 200 times the load of the rest (10 or more fires the rule), and a part needs another runtime. [high]

cells.text: All of it scaled for telemetry [med]

options.why: The same three rules: module boundaries do not give separate releases, separate scaling or a second runtime. [high]

options.label: Serverless functions

options.label: A few services
options.why: Several teams must react to the same vehicle events. With direct calls, telemetry would have to know each consumer, a new consumer would need a telemetry release, and a slow consumer would push back on the part with the highest load. [med]

Producer changes for each new consumer [med]

options.label: Services with an event backbone
options.why: The lowest option that survives the rules and the factors. It sits one rung above the lowest open option for one named reason: several teams must react to the same vehicle events. [high]

cells.text: Fits 2 platform engineers only with a managed broker and product teams on call [guess]
No cross-area transaction needed, and consumers accept that events arrive later [high]
A new consumer subscribes, and the producer does not change [med]
Broker, replays, event versions, tracing across async steps [med]
A broker to pay for. Relative only, no vendor chosen [med]

options.label: Microservices
options.why: 2 platform engineers, and at least 3 are needed for deployment, tracing and on-call across many services. [high]

cells.text: On-call and tooling per service, 2 platform engineers [high]
Most failure modes of the ladder [med]

blocks.text:
**The binding constraint is who can run it.** The next option up, microservices, is ruled out by a hard rule on people: the brief gives 2 platform engineers and the rule needs at least 3. With 4 teams and 5 business areas, nothing in the brief asks for many small services anyway. [high]

**The climb from a few services has one named reason.** Several teams must react to the same vehicle events (`fleet-platform.md:12`). With direct calls, the telemetry team would have to know every consumer, each new consumer would need a telemetry release, and a slow consumer would push back on the part with 200 times the load. That conflicts with teams shipping on their own schedules. [med]

**The bottom of the ladder is out for three separate reasons:** separate releases, the 200 times load and a second runtime. Removing only one of them changes nothing, which the rule re-runs confirmed. Serverless is out because route computations run for up to 40 minutes and load is steady. [high]

**Four deployables, not five.** Telemetry stands alone for its load and route optimisation for its runtime. The other two teams get one deployable each, so every team ships alone. Areas C and D share a deployable as separate modules, because nothing in the brief asks them to ship or scale apart. [med]

blocks.title: Thresholds the rules used
rows: one part takes 10 or more times the load of the rest
fires: one deployable and modular monolith out
work runs more than 15 minutes or holds state

blocks.text: These thresholds are the ruleset's judgements, not measurements, and on people the margin is one person. Two platform engineers cannot hold a day-and-night pager alone. If the product teams will not take on-call for their own services, this option fails on "can this team run it" as well, and the fix is more platform people, because every split shape needs someone on call. [med]

sections.title: What would change it
sections.intro: Each condition was checked by re-running the hard rules with that fact changed.

items: **Each event turns out to have one consumer.** Rule `nobody-to-notify` fires and leads to **a few services**.

**A third platform engineer joins.** Rule `too-few-platform-engineers` lifts and **microservices** is open again. It would still need a named reason, such as one team having to release parts of its area separately, and the brief has none today.

**A real transaction must span two areas.** Rule `one-transaction` rules out every split, and the one-deployable options are already out, so the ladder has no answer. Merge those two areas into one deployable, which keeps **this option** with one service fewer.

**All three reasons to split go away:** telemetry falls below 10 times the rest, route optimisation moves to .NET and the teams accept one release train. Rule `no-reason-to-split` fires and leaves the one-deployable options, and with 5 areas and 4 teams that means **a modular monolith**. Any one of these alone changes nothing.

rows: A script collects table names from every service's and module's migrations and checks each name has one owner. [med]

A telemetry project references the client of another service.
Each service has its own pipeline that builds from its own folder and tests against recorded contracts. A job compares each event schema with the last published version. [med]
A build needs another service's artifact, or an event schema breaks a published version.
Each service lists the services it calls in a manifest. CI builds the graph and looks for cycles. [med]
A route job outlives its worker
An integration test starts a job, kills the worker and checks that another worker finishes it from the checkpoint, and that the request was answered before the computation began. [med]

blocks.code:
# ADR-NNN: Build the fleet platform as services with an event backbone

Date: 2026-11-10
Status: Proposed

## Context
The fleet platform will be built by 30 engineers in 4 product teams, with 2
platform engineers. There are 5 business areas. The teams ship on their own
schedules. Vehicle telemetry ingestion takes about 200 times the load of the
rest. Route optimisation is in Python and the rest is .NET. Route computations
run for up to 40 minutes. Load is steady day and night. Several teams must react
to the same vehicle events. No transaction spans two business areas.

One deployable and a modular monolith are ruled out by separate releases, the
difference in load and the second runtime. Serverless functions are ruled out by
40-minute work and steady load. Microservices are ruled out by having 2 platform
engineers where 3 are needed. A few services without a backbone would make
telemetry call every consumer, so a new consumer would need a telemetry release.

## Decision
We will build services with an event backbone: four deployables around five
business areas.

- Telemetry ingestion and route optimisation each run alone. The other three
  areas run in two deployables, one per team, and two of them share a deployable
  as separate modules.
- Each service owns its data. No service writes another service's tables.
- Telemetry publishes derived vehicle events. Raw telemetry stays inside
  ingestion.
- Route computations are jobs: a request is accepted at once, a worker runs it,
  and the result is published as an event. A job resumes from a checkpoint after
  a lost worker.
- The broker is a managed service. Product teams are on call for their own
  services. The platform engineers run the broker, the deployment path and
  tracing.

## Consequences
Easier: each team ships alone, telemetry scales alone, and a new consumer
subscribes without a change to the producer.

Harder: eventual consistency between areas, event versioning and replays, and
tracing across asynchronous steps.

We accept: a broker that every team depends on, on-call duty in the product
teams, and two platform engineers with little slack.

We will revisit this if events stop being shared, if a transaction must span two
areas, or if the platform team reaches 3 or more and a team needs to release
parts of its area separately.

items: What are the other three business areas, and which team owns what? The answer settles whether there are four or five deployables.
Do other teams need raw telemetry or only derived vehicle events? Raw telemetry would put the 200 times load on the backbone.
What are the actual rates and retention? The brief gives only a ratio, so the broker and telemetry cannot be sized or priced yet.
Who takes the night pager? Load is steady day and night, and the brief does not say who is on call.
Can a route computation resume from a checkpoint? If not, a lost worker costs up to 40 minutes of work and deployments must wait for running jobs.
Must one vehicle's events arrive in order, and how far back must a consumer be able to replay?
How does this system relate to the code already in `acme-logistics`? Only the brief was read for this page.
